prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and the experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state in HgTe quantum wells.

statement.case_for: Topological insulators replaced the idea that electronic phases are classified only by broken symmetry with a classification by band topology, with protected edge and surface states. The chain is clear: Kane and Mele introduced the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall state, and Molenkamp's group delivered the decisive early transport observation of helical edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells. The result has been confirmed in many materials by transport, photoemission and scanning probes, and the concept has spread to photonics, cold atoms and superconducting-circuit proposals. The key papers are now almost two decades old, so the interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, arguably overdue. It is also distinct from the 2016 prize, which honoured topological phase transitions and Hall-type topological phases rather than time-reversal-invariant topological band insulators. Three of eight colleagues placed it first and five placed it in their top three, so I do not need to rely on my own ranking alone.
statement.case_against: The credit is genuinely contestable. The HgTe prediction that made Molenkamp's experiment possible came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who are not among the credited names, and the three-dimensional topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents, Hasan and others) is also outside this credit; I am working from my own recollection of these priority questions and have not verified them. A prize built on Kane-Mele and Molenkamp could therefore be read as leaving out the theory that directly enabled the key experiment. A second concern is overlap with the 2016 topology prize. Finally, applications have so far been limited, so the case is conceptual rather than technological, and a reader who values demonstrated device impact will find it thinner than the clock or quantum cascade laser cases.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the optical lattice clock first, as a clean idea with a measurable payoff and good timing, and ranked topological insulators only eighth, citing incomplete credit for Zhang, Bernevig, Hughes, Fu and Moore and his limited ability to judge condensed-matter details.
responses.response: I agree the credit problem is real and I do not wave it away, but it applies in some form to almost every shortlisted candidate, including the clock, where other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock lineage stand outside the two names. I place the clock second and would be content with it; my difference with Kroll is that the topological-insulator discovery has had a wider consequence for how condensed matter is classified, whereas the clock is a refinement of a precision-metrology programme already honoured in 2005 and 2012. I take his point that the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp trio is not self-evidently complete, and I would want the citation worded so that it describes what these three did rather than claiming the whole field.

responses.point: Lindroth put the clock first and topological insulators second, regarding the lattice clock as a separate and later achievement than the 2005 comb prize, and the topological-insulator case as a natural complement to 2016 that extends it to time-reversal-invariant systems.
responses.response: I accept her argument that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement from the comb, and that weakens the 'incremental' worry I raised myself on the clock; that is why it is my first alternative. Where I differ is on ranking: both are mature and well confirmed, but I judge the conceptual reach of band topology to be larger than that of a better clock. Her description of topological insulators as extending 2016 is, I think, the correct answer to the overlap objection, and I would use it in committee.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked topological insulators fourth, calling Kane and Mele the decisive theory and Molenkamp the experimental observation, but treating the omission of Zhang and Bernevig-Hughes as a real allocation problem and noting overlap with the 2016 prize; his first choice was the IceCube neutrino discovery.
responses.response: We agree on the facts and on the allocation difficulty; our disagreement is how much weight it carries. His own assessment says that within the credited names the trio is the strongest, and I think that is the relevant test for a committee limited to three laureates and to the names put before it. I also take the IceCube discovery seriously as an opening of a new observational window, but a one-name credit for a collaboration-scale discovery is a harder problem than the one facing B039, as Pearce also notes, and I would not let it outrank a three-person configuration with a clear theory-to-experiment chain.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked topological insulators first and stressed the theory-to-experiment chain, but raised whether the prize should centre on the 2D quantum spin Hall effect or on the 3D materials, and the risk of splitting the field.
responses.response: I side with centring the citation on the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification, because that is where the supplied three names have a decisive and demonstrable role; crediting the 3D case would widen it beyond what these names can carry. I share his worry about splitting the field, and for that reason I would prefer the committee treat the field as one prize rather than add a second topological part. Where I would press him is on whether magic-angle graphene, which he ranks second, is really mature enough to sit beside this one, since the pairing mechanism there is still unsettled.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranked IceCube first, calling the neutrino discovery an instrumentation achievement of the first rank, but regarded a single-name award as thin and arguably unfair to a collaboration; he ranked topological insulators fifth and noted he is less able to judge condensed-matter theory details.
responses.response: I share his reservation on the one-name credit, and I would add that the committee cannot repair it by adding names that are not on the shortlist. I respect his preference for the discovery-in-instrumentation case and I would not rule it out if a defensible multi-person credit could be established, but with the supplied credit I find it weaker than B039. On topological insulators, I would invite him to weigh the confirmation record, which is among the broadest of any candidate here, rather than to defer to condensed-matter specialists.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, or the 3D topological-insulator discoverers, have a claim strong enough that a citation naming only Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would be considered unfair; I have not verified the priority history.
Whether the committee regards the overlap with the 2016 topology prize as a reason to wait.
Whether the clock prize would be preferred as a cleaner two-person allocation if the committee judges the topological-insulator credit too contested.
Whether the quantum cascade laser should be viewed as physics or engineering, and how credit should be split among the Bell Labs authors; I ranked it fourth, below the clock.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for B039. For B023 (circuit QED), I disclose that I work in superconducting circuits and circuit/waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and have documented Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and a frequent co-author (Anton Frisk Kockum); Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself or at least flag this if B023 or any superconducting-circuit configuration became a serious option, which is why I do not include it in my configuration or alternatives.
